title: Chicago's Plantation and the great drummers, including the stick juggler
summary: Miller names drummers, praising one who juggled eight sticks while recording in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, I said yeah, yeah. Yeah, I said. When I first hit Chicago I went right away to playin' at the place called Plantation. Right straight there. Well who were some good jazz drummers? Well, David Doss, take him, he was pretty nice.
And you mean in New Orleans? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And, you mean in New Orleans?

The Chinese was not that bad drum. And, well, the Athens was strict, they used to call him the clock, you know, he kept the straight time. How pretty? William. He had a red happy hood in, he was bad man. And, little Chinese. Black Benner was pretty good. And, well, this happy over, no, Stutt is, he was a good drummer, but he didn't, you know, do much similar work and things like that. He did a lot of similar work?
He did a lot of similar work? He did not. He did not. Because he was a snare man. Yeah.
I like that to be a tough one.

But the best drummer, what I know was from me, I didn't ever play with him, I played with him in Chicago, with them snags. He'd do so much with them sticks, you know, and the boys would take eight sticks, and use every one of them, eight. It's funny, but he did it, put two in his back pockets, two in his side pockets, one on his chin, two in his hand, and one in his shirt pocket. And play and don't miss nothing, get a stick every now and then, get him out of his back pocket.

He didn't miss anything. He played a drum on that record with me in the basement, where he was, Shine. Yeah, I know the one. You heard it, well, he played it, he was doing all that with them sticks then.
While he was making the record he was doing it.
It doesn't come through on the record, of course, you'd never know he was doing that.
